claim: In the clausal complement of with or without, a gerund-participial cannot take a genitive subject.
evidence_summary: CGEL itself treats without as part of the construction (n. 61; [23id]). Edited prose: Owens (2012) without my having communicated; Thomasson (2015) without their being governed by the standard rules of use; Mill without our being aware of it.
finding: Genitive subjects occur after without. The restriction may hold for absolute with, as in With me out of the way.
proposed_wording: In the absolute construction with with, a gerund-participial cannot take a genitive subject. After without a genitive subject is possible.
inference: Does without exclude a genitive subject in its gerund-participial complement?

evidence.passage: §16.2.1(f), p. 461. “this is one place where a gerund-participial in complement function cannot take a genitive subject”.
evidence.example: Footnote 61 and [23id] place without in the construction.
evidence.establishes: The restriction is stated for both prepositions.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.

evidence.source: David Owens (2012). Shaping the Normative Landscape, “The Promissory Bond”. Oxford University Press.
evidence.establishes: A genitive subject with a perfect gerund-participial after without.

evidence.source: Amie L. Thomasson (2015). Ontology Made Easy. Oxford University Press. ISBN 978-0-19-938511-9.

evidence.establishes: A genitive subject with a passive gerund-participial after without.
